title: Human Health and Disease
description: Grade 12 Biology: health and common human diseases, the immune system and vaccination, and AIDS, cancer and drug and alcohol abuse.

topics.title: Health and Common Human Diseases
topics.concept:
Health is not just the absence of disease — it is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being. Good health lets a person work efficiently and enjoy life. Disease is any condition that disturbs the normal working of the body or mind.

Diseases are broadly of two kinds: infectious (communicable) diseases, caused by germs (pathogens) and spread from one person to another, and non-infectious diseases, which are not spread by germs (like cancer or genetic disorders).

Infectious diseases are caused by different kinds of pathogens:

  • Bacteria — e.g. typhoid, tuberculosis (TB), cholera, pneumonia.
  • Viruses — e.g. the common cold, influenza, dengue, chikungunya, AIDS.
  • Protozoa — e.g. malaria (caused by Plasmodium, spread by the female Anopheles mosquito) and amoebiasis.
  • Fungi — e.g. ringworm and other skin diseases.
  • Worms (helminths) — e.g. Ascaris (roundworm) and filaria.

Pathogens spread through air, water, food, contact, or via vectors (carriers) like mosquitoes and houseflies. Good hygiene (clean water, proper sanitation, washing hands, controlling mosquitoes) and vaccination are the main ways to prevent infectious diseases.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is health, according to its full definition?
examples.solution:
Health is more than the absence of disease.

  • It is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being.
examples.answer: Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not just the absence of disease.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name the pathogen and the vector of malaria.
examples.solution:
Malaria is a protozoan disease.

  • Pathogen: Plasmodium (a protozoan).
  • Vector: the female Anopheles mosquito.
examples.answer: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium (a protozoan) and spread by the female Anopheles mosquito.

examples.problem: Example 3: Give two ways to prevent infectious diseases.
examples.solution:
Focus on hygiene and immunity.

  • Maintain hygiene (clean water, sanitation, controlling vectors).
  • Get vaccinated.
examples.answer: Maintaining good hygiene (clean water, sanitation, vector control) and getting vaccinated.

recap:
• Health = complete physical, mental and social well-being; disease disturbs normal functioning.
  • Infectious (germs, spread) vs non-infectious (e.g. cancer, genetic).
  • Pathogens: bacteria (TB, typhoid, cholera), viruses (cold, dengue, AIDS), protozoa (malaria — Plasmodium/Anopheles), fungi, worms.
  • Prevent: hygiene + vaccination; spread by air/water/food/contact/vectors.

quiz.explanation: Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium.

quiz.q: Diseases caused by germs and spread from person to person are:
quiz.explanation: Infectious diseases are caused by pathogens and are communicable.

topics.title: The Immune System and Vaccination
topics.concept:
The body has a built-in defence system — the immune system — that protects it against pathogens. Immunity is the ability of the body to resist or fight infection. There are two broad types:

  • Innate (natural) immunity — present from birth; it gives general, non-specific defence. It includes barriers like the skin, mucus and stomach acid, and cells like white blood cells that engulf germs.
  • Acquired (adaptive) immunity — developed during life after exposure to a particular pathogen; it is specific and has memory, so the body responds faster on a second exposure.

Acquired immunity works mainly through antibodies — special proteins made by white blood cells (lymphocytes) that recognise and bind to a particular germ (the antigen) and help destroy it. Because of memory cells, once you have fought off a germ you are often protected against it in future.

Vaccination (immunisation) uses this principle. A vaccine contains a weakened or killed germ (or part of it) that cannot cause disease but does trigger the immune system to make antibodies and memory cells. So if the real germ attacks later, the body destroys it quickly — the person is immune. Vaccines have controlled or wiped out many deadly diseases (for example, smallpox has been eradicated and polio nearly so). Giving ready-made antibodies (as in an anti-snake-venom injection) is passive immunity, which acts at once but does not last.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is the difference between innate and acquired immunity?
examples.solution:
One is present from birth, the other develops.

  • Innate: present from birth, general/non-specific (skin, WBCs).
  • Acquired: develops after exposure, specific, with memory.
examples.answer: Innate immunity is present from birth and non-specific; acquired immunity develops after exposure, is specific and has memory.

examples.solution:
They fight specific germs.

  • Antibodies are proteins made by lymphocytes.
  • They recognise and bind a specific antigen to help destroy it.
examples.answer: Antibodies are proteins made by white blood cells that recognise and bind a specific germ (antigen) to help destroy it.

examples.problem: Example 3: How does a vaccine protect against disease?
examples.solution:
It trains the immune system.

  • A vaccine has a weakened/killed germ that triggers antibodies and memory cells without causing disease.
  • If the real germ attacks later, the body destroys it quickly.
examples.answer: A vaccine triggers the immune system to make antibodies and memory cells, so the real germ is destroyed quickly later.

recap:
• Immunity = ability to resist infection: innate (from birth, non-specific: skin, WBCs) and acquired (specific, has memory).
  • Antibodies (proteins from lymphocytes) bind a specific antigen.
  • Vaccination: weakened/killed germ → antibodies + memory cells → immunity (smallpox eradicated).
  • Ready-made antibodies = passive immunity (fast, short-lived).

quiz.q: Proteins made by the body that bind to specific germs are:
quiz.explanation: Antibodies bind specific antigens to help destroy germs.

quiz.q: A vaccine works by making the body produce:
quiz.explanation: Vaccines trigger antibodies and memory cells for future protection.

topics.title: AIDS, Cancer and Drug Abuse
topics.concept:
Some serious health problems deserve special mention.

AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome) is caused by the HIV virus, which attacks and weakens the immune system (especially certain white blood cells). As immunity collapses, the person falls prey to many infections. HIV spreads through unprotected sex, infected blood or shared needles, and from an infected mother to her baby — not by casual contact like shaking hands or sharing food. There is no complete cure yet, so prevention (safe practices, screened blood, clean needles, awareness) is vital.

Cancer is a non-infectious disease in which some cells lose control over their division and multiply uncontrollably, forming a mass called a tumour. A malignant tumour can spread to other parts of the body (a process called metastasis), which makes cancer dangerous. Cancer can be caused by certain chemicals (carcinogens, such as those in tobacco smoke), radiation and some viruses. Tobacco use is a major preventable cause. Early detection (screening) and treatments like surgery, radiation and chemotherapy can save lives.

Drug and alcohol abuse means the harmful, non-medical use of drugs and alcohol. Commonly abused substances include opioids (like heroin), cannabis, cocaine and alcohol; many are addictive, meaning the body craves them. Abuse damages health, behaviour, studies, family and society. Warning signs include falling performance, mood swings and withdrawal from friends and family. Prevention and help include avoiding peer pressure, seeking support from parents and teachers, counselling and rehabilitation. Saying "no" to drugs and leading a healthy, active life is the best protection.

examples.problem: Example 1: What causes AIDS, and how does it harm the body?
examples.solution:
AIDS is a viral disease.

  • It is caused by the HIV virus.
  • HIV attacks and weakens the immune system, so the body cannot fight other infections.
examples.answer: AIDS is caused by the HIV virus, which weakens the immune system so the body cannot fight off infections.

examples.problem: Example 2: What makes a malignant tumour dangerous?
examples.solution:
It can spread.

  • A malignant tumour can spread to other parts of the body (metastasis).
examples.answer: A malignant tumour can spread to other parts of the body (metastasis), which makes cancer dangerous.

examples.problem: Example 3: Give two ways to prevent drug and alcohol abuse.
examples.solution:
Focus on avoidance and support.

  • Avoid peer pressure and say no to drugs.
  • Seek support from parents/teachers and counselling.
examples.answer: Avoiding peer pressure (saying no) and seeking support/counselling from parents, teachers or professionals.

recap:
• AIDS: caused by HIV, weakens immunity; spreads via unsafe sex, infected blood/needles, mother→baby (NOT casual contact); no cure → prevention.
  • Cancer: uncontrolled cell division → tumour; malignant spreads (metastasis); causes: carcinogens (tobacco), radiation, some viruses.
  • Drug/alcohol abuse: harmful, addictive; damages health/society; prevent via avoiding peer pressure, counselling, healthy life.

quiz.explanation: AIDS is caused by the HIV virus, which weakens immunity.

quiz.q: The spread of cancer cells to other parts of the body is called:
quiz.explanation: Metastasis is the spread of malignant tumour cells.

questions.q: Health is best defined as:
options: Complete physical, mental and social well-being
questions.explanation: Health is complete physical, mental and social well-being.

questions.q: Diseases spread from person to person by germs are:
questions.explanation: Infectious (communicable) diseases are spread by pathogens.

questions.q: Tuberculosis and typhoid are caused by:
questions.explanation: TB and typhoid are bacterial diseases.

questions.q: Which disease is caused by a virus?
questions.explanation: Dengue is a viral disease.

questions.q: Malaria is spread by the:
questions.explanation: The female Anopheles mosquito spreads malaria.

questions.q: Immunity present from birth and non-specific is:
questions.explanation: Innate immunity is present from birth and general.

questions.q: Proteins that bind specific antigens are:
questions.explanation: Antibodies bind specific antigens.

questions.q: A vaccine contains a weakened or killed germ that triggers:
questions.explanation: Vaccines trigger antibodies and memory cells without causing disease.

questions.q: Which disease has been completely eradicated by vaccination?
questions.explanation: Smallpox has been eradicated worldwide.

questions.q: Giving ready-made antibodies (e.g. anti-venom) provides:
questions.explanation: Ready-made antibodies give fast but short-lived passive immunity.

questions.q: AIDS is caused by:
questions.explanation: HIV causes AIDS by weakening immunity.

questions.q: HIV does NOT spread through:
questions.explanation: HIV does not spread by casual contact.

questions.q: Uncontrolled division of cells forming a mass is a:
questions.explanation: Uncontrolled cell division forms a tumour (cancer).

questions.q: Cancer-causing agents are called:
questions.explanation: Carcinogens cause cancer (e.g. tobacco smoke).

questions.q: A good way to prevent drug abuse is to:
options: Avoid peer pressure and seek support
questions.explanation: Avoiding peer pressure and seeking support help prevent abuse.

questions.q: Chikungunya, like dengue, is a viral disease spread by:
questions.explanation: Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne viral disease.

questions.q: Draining stagnant water and using mosquito nets fights malaria mainly by:
questions.explanation: Removing breeding sites and avoiding bites controls the Anopheles vector that carries the parasite.

questions.q: A second infection by the same germ is often milder because acquired immunity has:
questions.explanation: Memory cells from the first exposure mount a quicker, stronger response on re-exposure.

questions.q: Vaccination protects a whole community partly through herd immunity, which means:
options: When most people are immune, the germ spreads less to everyone
questions.explanation: High immunity in the population breaks transmission chains, indirectly protecting the unvaccinated too.

questions.q: AIDS makes a person prone to many other infections because HIV:
options: Destroys immune cells that fight infection
questions.explanation: By killing key immune cells, HIV leaves the body unable to defend against other pathogens.

questions.q: Quitting tobacco reduces cancer risk because tobacco smoke contains:
questions.explanation: Carcinogens in smoke trigger the cell changes that lead to cancer, so avoiding them lowers risk.

questions.q: Early detection (screening) improves cancer survival mainly because it allows treatment before the tumour:
questions.explanation: Treating a localised tumour before metastasis is far more successful than after it spreads.
